name: sb_lower_bound (Fastest Branchless Binary Search)
workload: Branchless lower_bound over sorted arrays of primitive integer types and over arrays of 8-byte strings, average ns/call across a benchmark suite
claimed_speedup: 33.24 ns vs std::lower_bound's 61.30 ns on primitive types (~2x); geometric mean 19.81 ns vs 39.17 ns across the suite; roughly a wash (162.68 ns vs 157.71 ns, slightly slower) for 8-byte string keys
compiler_and_flags: g++-10 / clang++-10, -std=c++20 -Wall -O2 -march=haswell (some clang runs additionally used -mllvm -x86-cmov-converter=false)
tradeoffs: Branchless codegen depends on cmov being emitted, so results are compiler/flag sensitive; gains shrink or reverse for expensive comparators (e.g. string keys); needs random-access iterators
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (usability=reference, not safe to copy verbatim without contacting the author); benchmark is the author's own, run on a single CPU (Kaby Lake) only; small project (24 stars), last pushed mid-2023.

name: SIMD Quad search (Lemire blog benchmark)
workload: Membership queries on sorted arrays of 16-bit unsigned integers, sizes 2-4096 elements, 100,000 arrays per size, 10M cold-cache queries + 10M warm-cache queries per size, on Roaring-Bitmap-style array containers
claimed_speedup: "more than twice as fast" as std::binary_search in every tested configuration: >2x on warm cache on Intel Emerald Rapids/GCC, >2x on cold cache on Apple M4/Apple LLVM; also beats std::find (linear search) and a binary-search-plus-SIMD variant lacking the quaternary interpolation step
compiler_and_flags: GCC (Intel Emerald Rapids run), Apple LLVM/clang (Apple M4 run); exact optimization flags not printed in the post itself; benchmark driver source confirms the calls are literally std::binary_search(arr.begin(), arr.end(), k) and std::find(arr.begin(), arr.end(), k) != arr.end()
hardware: Intel Emerald Rapids server CPU; Apple M4
stars_or_usage: 962 stars (whole blog-code monorepo, not this snippet alone)
tradeoffs: Specialized to 16-bit-unsigned-integer arrays laid out in fixed 16-element blocks (built for Roaring Bitmap array containers), needs NEON or SSE2; the quaternary-interpolation half of the trick only pays off on the Intel platform per the author's own three-way ablation, not on Apple M4
caveats: Single-author blog benchmark, not a packaged/versioned library -- the whole implementation is a ~20-line function given in the post's appendix; no LICENSE file in the monorepo; exact -O flags for the two machines are not stated in the post; only two machines tested.

name: scandum/binary_search (monobound / boundless binary search)
workload: 32-bit integer sorted arrays, sizes from 1 to 10 million elements; 1,000-10,000 iterations per size, best-of run timed
claimed_speedup: Monobound binary search: 2-4x faster than a standard/textbook binary search on arrays smaller than 1M 32-bit ints, and up to 60% faster than libc's bsearch(); boundless binary search: roughly 20% faster than standard binary search on 32-bit ints
hardware: Intel i3 quad-core, under WSL2 (exact CPU model/SKU not given)

caveats: Baseline is C's bsearch() and a generic 'textbook' binary search, not std::lower_bound/std::binary_search directly, so this is an indirect (but explicitly named) comparison; CPU model is imprecise ('i3 quad-core'); all numbers come from one 2018-era Ubuntu/GCC 7.5 machine.

name: sse4-strstr (SIMD substring search, Mula)
workload: Locate every word from a word list (data/words) inside a text corpus (data/i386.txt); cumulative match-position checksum verified identical across kernels, best-of-3 timed runs
claimed_speedup: On the Skylake i7-6700 / GCC 5.4.1 result file: AVX2 (generic) kernel 0.364s vs std::strstr 0.662s (~1.8x faster); other kernels on the same file range from slower than std::strstr (SWAR 64-bit generic: 1.404s, SSE4.2 PCMPESTRM: 1.391s) to faster (SSE2 generic: 0.489s, AVX2 MPSADBW: 0.570s)
compiler_and_flags: g++ -std=c++11 -O3 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -mavx2 -DHAVE_AVX2_INSTRUCTIONS -DNDEBUG (Makefile's speedup_avx2 target); GCC 5.4.1 for the cited result; the results/ directory also has GCC 4.8-7.4 and Clang 3.8 runs on other CPUs
hardware: Intel Core i7-6700 (Skylake) for the cited number; results/ additionally covers ARMv7, ARMv8 (Clang), AMD Bulldozer FX-8510, Intel Haswell i7-4770, Knights Landing 7210, Skylake i9-7900, and Westmere
tradeoffs: Kernels require SSE4.1/SSE4.2/AVX2/AVX-512 at compile time with no runtime CPU dispatch in this benchmark harness; only does byte-string needle-in-haystack search, not the generic iterator/predicate-based std::search; not every SIMD kernel beats std::strstr on every CPU in this repo's own results
caveats: Companion sample code for a 2016-era article on SIMD substring search; last committed January 2022 (abandoned). The ~1.8x figure is for one specific kernel/CPU pairing -- results vary widely by kernel and machine in the repo's own results/ files. std::strstr is the C-string facility imported into namespace std, not literally the generic std::search named for this category, though it performs the same substring-search job.

name: simdsearch (Needle-Hammer)
workload: Substring search over ordinary text at memory speed; needle-in-haystack throughput measured on an Apple M-series core
claimed_speedup: About 45 GB/s on an Apple M-series core, roughly 30x the platform's memmem
compiler_and_flags: GCC 14/15 or Apple clang 17 (library is C++17, benchmark driver needs C++23 for std::print); g++ -std=c++17 -O2 -mavx512f -mavx512bw on x86-64, plain -O2 on AArch64; tuning constants were fitted on Emerald Rapids, Zen 5 and Apple M4 Max
hardware: An unspecified 'Apple M-series core' for the headline 45 GB/s/30x figure; AVX-512F+BW required on x86-64, NEON on AArch64
tradeoffs: x86-64 build requires AVX-512F+BW at compile time with no runtime fallback (illegal instruction on CPUs without it, which excludes most Intel client parts and pre-Zen4 AMD); MSVC unsupported; benchmarked against C-library memmem/strstr, StringZilla and SSEF rather than against std::search
caveats: No LICENSE file in the repo (reference usability only); the '45 GB/s, 30x memmem' figure names only an 'Apple M-series core', not an exact chip, and the README itself says benchmark numbers should be measured on your own machine rather than trusted from CI; baseline is the C library's memmem, not the C++ std::search named for this category, though it performs the same job.
